title: Chinese Landscape Painting
objective: After this level you can explain how Chinese painters used ink to capture mountains and mist.
summary: Shan shui ("mountain-water") painting flowered in the Northern Song. Fan Kuan dwarfed his travelers under a huge mountain; Guo Xi combined three distances; mist is often bare silk.

cards.headline: The most famous landscape in China hid its painter's name for centuries.
cards.body: It's called Travelers among Mountains and Streams, and the painter is Fan Kuan. You'll need a moment to find the travelers. Finding his signature took scholars far longer.

cards.headline: A mountain, and some very small people
cards.body: Fan Kuan painted it about 1000, in ink on a silk hanging scroll over 2 meters tall. A huge mountain fills most of the picture. The travelers are a tiny mule train near the bottom. In 1958, a scholar at the National Palace Museum in Taipei spotted Fan Kuan's signature hidden among the leaves beside the mules. The artist, too, made himself small.

cards.headline: Mountain-water
cards.body: The Chinese term for landscape painting, shan shui, means "mountain-water". Monumental landscapes like Fan Kuan's flowered in the Northern Song dynasty (960–1127). The court painter Guo Xi wrote of three distances: high, looking up at a peak; deep, peering into the valleys behind; and level, gazing across to far hills. His Early Spring of 1072 combines all three. Your eye doesn't stand still. It goes for a walk.

cards.fact: In Chinese landscapes, the mist is often just bare silk.
cards.context: Painters paid as much attention to the unpainted parts of a picture as to the painted ones. Mist and cloud are often simply silk or paper left empty, and your eye fills them with air. Remember Level 3's negative space, the empty part with a shape of its own? Here the emptiness does some of the heaviest work.

mascot.line: The cheapest part of the painting is the mist. Also, arguably, the hardest part to get right.

cards.headline: Mountain-water: painted
learned: Fan Kuan's travelers are a tiny mule train
Guo Xi combined three distances in one picture
Mist is often bare silk: negative space at work

questions.prompt: In Fan Kuan's Travelers among Mountains and Streams, where are the travelers?

options.label: A tiny mule train near the bottom
Large figures in the center
options.rationale: The center belongs to the huge mountain.

options.label: Boats crossing a lake at the top
options.rationale: The travelers are a mule train at the bottom.

options.label: Hidden inside the mist
options.rationale: The signature is hidden; the travelers are at the bottom.

questions.explanation: A huge mountain fills most of the scroll; the travelers are a tiny mule train near the bottom.

questions.prompt: What do Guo Xi's "three distances" let a landscape painting do?

options.label: Show a scene exactly as a camera would
options.rationale: A camera has one viewpoint; this combines three.

options.label: Measure mountains to the correct scale
options.rationale: The idea is about viewpoints, not measurement.

options.label: Combine several viewpoints in one picture
Paint only what is far away
options.rationale: It includes high, deep and level views together.

questions.explanation: Guo Xi's high, deep and level distances combine in one picture, so your eye moves instead of standing at one fixed point.

questions.prompt: Level 3 said empty space has a shape too. How do Chinese landscape painters often show mist?

options.label: With thick white paint
options.rationale: The mist is usually left unpainted.

options.label: By leaving the silk or paper bare
With dots of gold leaf
options.rationale: Gold belongs to Byzantine mosaics, not these landscapes.

options.label: By painting a separate scroll
options.rationale: It's in the same picture, as empty space.

questions.explanation: Mist and cloud are often bare silk or paper: negative space doing real work.
